conservator.e: From Middle English conservatour, from Anglo-Norman conservatour, from Latin cōnservātor (“one who conserves”), agent noun from cōnservō (“to preserve”).

d.g: Having the quality of preserving from loss, decay, or injury.
Relating to conservation.
A storehouse.
A large greenhouse or hothouse for the display of plants

conservatory.e: English conserve English -ate English -ory English -atory English conservatory From conserve + -atory. Doublet of conservatoire.

d.g: Wilderness where human development is prohibited.
A jam or thick syrup made from fruit.
d.x: I shall […] study broths, plasters, and conserves, till from a fine lady I become a notable woman.

d.g: To save for later use, sometimes by the use of a preservative.
d.x: to conserve fruits with sugar

d.g: To protect an environment, heritage, etc.

conserve.e: From Middle English conserven, from Old French conserver, from Latin conservare (“to keep, preserve”), from com- (intensive prefix) + servo (“keep watch, maintain”). See also observe.

d.g: plural of conserve
third-person singular simple present indicative of conserve
The characteristic of being considerate.

considerateness.e: English considerate Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English considerateness From considerate + -ness.

d.g: The thought process of considering, of taking multiple or specified factors into account (with of being the main corresponding adposition).
d.x: After much consideration, I have decided to stay.

d.g: Something considered as a reason or ground for a (possible) decision.
d.x: Speculations about the possible entire reconstruction of society give the intellectual fare much more to his taste than the more practical and short-run considerations of those who aim at a piecemeal improvement of the existing order.

d.g: The tendency to consider others and make allowances for their needs or desires.
d.x: You showed remarkable consideration in giving up your place for your friend.

d.g: A payment or other recompense for something done.
d.x: Sure I'll move my car, but only for a consideration.

consideration.e: From Middle English consideracioun, from Old French consideracion, from Latin cōnsīderātiō. By surface analysis, consider + -ation.

d.g: The person to whom a shipment is to be delivered.
One to whom anything is consigned or entrusted.
d.x: The letter had been given to the two Englishmen by a good friend of theirs in London, who had been in America two years previously, and had singled out Mr. J. L. Westgate from the many friends he had left there as the consignee, as it were, of his compatriots.

consignee.e: English consign English -ee English consignee From consign + -ee.

d.g: The party that consigns.
The party that provides merchandise for consignment sale.
d.x: The two joined Mr. Hook and the consigner at dinner to discuss the sale and then returned to the house.

consigner.e: English consign Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English consigner From consign + -er.

d.g: A collection of goods to be sent, in transit or having been sent.
d.x: In order to provide for a large measure of rail participation in countrywide collection and delivery of small consignments—a task they were never particularly well suited to do, and which they did only because the horse and cart were worse—the railways sacrificed their main advantages.

d.g: The act of consigning.

The sale of one's own goods (clothing, furniture, etc.) through a third-party vendor, in exchange for a portion of the sale price, and with the consigner retaining ownership of the goods until they are sold or abandoned.

consignment.e: English consign Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -mentbor. Middle English -ment English -ment English consignment From consign + -ment.

d.g: Alternative form of consigner.
d.x: Catalogues for evening auctions frequently devote a section to art consigned from one collection, with several pages praising the consignor.

consignor.e: English consign English -or English consignor From consign + -or.

d.g: Logical consistency; lack of self-contradiction.
The staying together, or remaining in close relation, of non-physical things.
d.x: Her performance has lacked consistence over the last year.

d.g: A substance which adheres together.

consistence.e: From Middle French. Compare French consistance. By surface analysis, consist + -ence.

d.g: Local coherence.
Correspondence or compatibility.
Reliability or uniformity; the quality of being consistent.
d.x: They want to achieve a high degree of consistency in their process and their product.

d.g: The degree of viscosity of something.
d.x: Mix it until it has the consistency of a thick paste.

d.g: Freedom from contradiction; the state of a system of axioms such that none of the propositions deduced from them are mutually contradictory.

consistency.e: By surface analysis, consistent + -cy, consistence + -y or consist + -ency.

d.g: A solemn assembly or council.
d.x: To council summons all his mighty peers, / Within thick clouds and dark tenfold involved, / A gloomy consistory.

d.g: The spiritual court of a diocesan bishop held before his chancellor or commissioner in his cathedral church or elsewhere.
An assembly of prelates; a session of the College of Cardinals at Rome.
d.x: Pius […][was] then hearing of causes in consistory.

d.g: A church tribunal or governing body, especially of elders in a Reformed church.

consistory.e: Inherited from Middle English consistorie, from Old Northern French consistorie (“secular tribunal”) (Old French consistoire), and Late Latin consistorium (“waiting room, meeting place of the imperial council”). Meaning "Church council" is from early 14th century. By surface analysis, consist + -ory.

d.g: The act or example of consoling; the condition of being consoled.
d.x: [I]f Charles is undone, He'll find half his Acquaintance ruin'd too, and that, you know, is a consolation—

d.g: The prize or benefit for the loser.
A consolation goal.

consolation.e: From Old French consolacion (French consolatio), from Latin cōnsōlātiō, from the deponent verb cōnsōlor (“I console, encourage”) with the -tiō suffix, while cōnsōlor comprises the intensifying prefix con- with the deponent verb sōlor (“I comfort, console”). Equivalent to console + -ation. Doublet of consolatio.

d.g: A stand-alone cabinet designed to stand on the floor; especially, one integrated with home entertainment equipment, such as a TV or stereo system.
d.x: The film's music blared from the console.

d.g: A desk-like cabinet, table, or stand upon which controls, instruments, and displays are mounted.
An instrument with displays and an input device that is used to monitor and control an electronic system.
The keyboard and screen of a computer or other electronic device.

console.e: Borrowed from French console (“bracket”, noun), from consoler (“to console, to comfort”, verb). Sense of “bracket” either due to a bracket alleviating the load, or due to brackets being decorated with the Christian figure of a consolateur (“consoler”), itself perhaps a pun on the first sense (alleviating load). Originally used for the bracket itself, then for wall-mounted tables (mounted with a bracket), then for free-standing tables placed against a wall.

d.g: plants having flowers resembling the larkspur's but differing from larkspur's in the arrangement of petals;  sometimes included in genus Delphinium
The act or process of consolidating, making firm, or uniting; the state of being consolidated.
The combination of several actions into one.
A solidification into a firm dense mass. It is usually applied to induration (swelling or hardening of normally soft tissue) of a normally aerated lung.
d.x: The areas of lung dysventilation with an absence of alveolar air are visualized in the form of consolidations adjacent to the pleural line.

consolidation.e: From Latin cōnsolidātiō, cōnsolidātiōnem, from cōnsolidō.

d.g: Alternative spelling of consommé.
A form of rhyme having the same consonants but different vowels.
Harmony; agreement; absence of discordance.
d.x: Like a musical string, the optic nerve responds to the waves with which it is in consonance, while it refuses to be excited by others of almost infinitely greater energy, whose period of recurrence are not in unison with its own.

consonance.e: From Middle English consonance, from Middle French consonance, from Latin cōnsonantia. Doublet of consonancy. By surface analysis, con- + son- + -ance.

d.g: The spouse of a monarch.
d.x: Wise, just, moderate, admirably pure of life, the friend of science, of freedom, of peace and all peaceful arts, the Consort of the Queen passes from our troubled sphere to that serene one where justice and peace reign eternal.

d.g: A husband, wife, companion or partner.
d.x: In his death was lost to his consort an affectionate and beloved husband; […]

d.g: An informal, usually well-publicized sexual companion of a monarch, aristocrat, celebrity, etc.
A ship accompanying another.

consort.e: Borrowed from Middle French, ultimately from Latin cōnsors. As “companion or partner”, via Middle English consorte.

d.g: An association or combination of businesses, financial institutions, or investors, for the purpose of engaging in a joint venture.
A similar arrangement among non-commercial institutions or organizations.
d.x: We wanted to share that kind thought with you because today, November 13, is "World Kindness Day" — created back in 1998 by a consortium of kindhearted charities.

d.g: An association or society.
The right of a spouse to all the normal relationships with his or her mate.

consortium.e: Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm Proto-Italic *kom Proto-Italic *kom- Latin con- Proto-Indo-European *ser-der. Proto-Italic *sortis Latin sors Latin cōnsors Proto-Indo-European *-yós Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -ius Latin -ium Latin cōnsortiumlbor. …

d.g: A detailed survey or overview of a subject.
d.x: Already the whole of his past life had vividly presented itself to him—myriads of tiny incidents, long forgotten, now standing out sharply in their due sequence. He had mastered this conspectus in a flash of time, and was already tired of it.

d.g: Openness or exposure to the view; a state of being clearly visible.
The property of being clearly discernible by the mind; obviousness.
Eminence; celebrity; renown.

conspicuousness.e: English conspicuous Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English conspicuousness From conspicuous + -ness.

d.g: An agreement or arrangement between multiple parties to do something harmful, immoral or subversive; an instance of collusion.
d.x: Conspiracies, like all other exercises of human ingenuity, are of very different kinds. The gloomy plots arranged in old Italian halls...

d.g: An agreement between two or more persons to break the law at some time in the future.
A secret agreement to do something.
d.x: Have you been part of a surprise party conspiracy or plotted a delightful treat for someone you love?

d.g: An agreement to work together to bring something about; an act or instance of conspiring.
d.x: When collaboration is conscious, planned, and shared with others, excitement builds and a conspiracy develops.

d.g: A group of ravens.
A group of lemurs.
d.x: Indeed, as I sat, forlorn, never having found my particular conspiracy of lemurs (how about that for a name for a group of lemurs? The name lemur itself comes from the Latin for “spirits of the dead”) …

d.g: To conspire.
d.x: He knew I would come for him when I discovered what he did, so he, he conspiracied to put me in prison.

conspiracy.e: From Middle English conspiracie, from Anglo-Norman conspiracie, from Latin cōnspīrātiō, from conspire + -acy. Doublet of conspiration.

d.g: One of a group that acts in harmony to do something unlawful and unethical; a person who is part of a conspiracy.
d.x: The conspirators were rounded up by the police and arrested.

d.g: One holding the lowest rank in most Commonwealth police forces. (See also chief constable.)
d.x: As soon as Julia returned with a constable, Timothy, who was on the point of exhaustion, prepared to give over to him gratefully. The newcomer turned out to be a powerful youngster, fully trained and eager to help, and he stripped off his tunic at once.

d.g: A police officer or an officer with equivalent powers.
An officer of a noble court in the Middle Ages, usually a senior army commander. (See also marshal).
The warden of a castle.

constable.e: From Middle English constable, cunstable, constabil, connestable, cunestable, from Old French conestable, from Latin comes stabulī (“officer of the stables”). For the sense-development; compare marshal. Doublet of connétable.

d.g: Of or relating to constables.
Characteristic of police; police-like, rather than military.
d.x: Constabulary missions are different from fighting wars.

d.g: A police force.
The police in a particular district or area.
d.x: As Hiro is entering their neighborhood, he sees men running down the undulating pontoon bridge that serves as the main street, carrying guns and knives. The local constabulary.

constabulary.e: From mediaeval Latin conestabularia, a noun use of the feminine version of conestabularius, from Latin constabulus, from comes stabuli, literally ‘master of the stables’.

d.g: a lake in southeastern Germany on the northern side of the Swiss Alps;  forms part of the Rhine River

constance.e: Derived from Latin Cōnstantia. Doublet of Constantia.

d.g: The quality of being constant; steadiness or faithfulness in action, affections, purpose, etc.
d.x:
A little Water cleares vs of this deed.
How eaſie is it then? your Conſtancie
Hath left you vnattended.

d.g: An unchanging quality or characteristic of a person or thing.
d.x:
[…] yonger ſpirits, […]
whoſe conſtancies
Expire before their faſhions: […]

constancy.e: Latin cōnstantiabor. English constancy Borrowed from Latin cōnstantia.

d.g: An alloy of copper and nickel whose resistivity is constant over a wide temperature range.
a Romanian resort city on the Black Sea

constantina.e: From Latin Cōnstantīna and Greek Κωνσταντίνα (Konstantína).

d.g: Emperor of Rome who stopped the persecution of Christians and in 324 made Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire;  in 330 he moved his capital from Rome to Byzantium and renamed it Constantinople (280-337)

constantine.e: From Latin Cōnstantīnus, the name of Roman emperors, notably that of Constantine the Great, Latin cōnstāns (“constant, steadfast”). Doublet of Konstadinos.

d.g: the largest city and former capital of Turkey;  rebuilt on the site of ancient Byzantium by Constantine I in the fourth century;  renamed Constantinople by Constantine who made it the capital of the Byzantine Empire;  now the seat of the Eastern Orthodox Church

constantinople.e: From Middle English Constantinople, ultimately from Late Latin Cōnstantīnopolis, from Ancient Greek Κωνσταντινούπολις (Kōnstantinoúpolis, “City of Constantine”), after Roman emperor Flavius Valerius Aurelius Constantinus (also known as Constantine I, St. Constantine, and/or Constantine the Great).

d.g: The process of verification.
An assertion; a proposition assumed for the sake of argument, an axiom.
d.x: From that constatation which is similar to the constatation that the human rights system expresses the views of the dominant group, Kymlicka concludes the need for cultural accommodation.

d.g: An arbitrary formation of stars perceived as a figure (especially one from mythology) or pattern, or a division of the sky including it, especially one officially recognized by astronomers; an asterism.
d.x: Harpa Georgii, or the Harp of George, is a new constellation introduced on the maps by one of the German astronomers, in honour of the late king of England, George III.

d.g: Any of the 88 regions of the sky officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union, including all stars and celestial bodies in the region.
A configuration or grouping of related things.
A wide, seemingly unlimited, assortment.
d.x: a constellation of possibilities

d.g: The configuration of planets at a given time (especially a person's birth), as believed to affect events on Earth, or used for determining a horoscope.
d.x: But alas such peruerse constellation nowe reigneth ouer men, that where some be aptely and naturally disposed to amitie, and fyndeth one, in similitude of studie and maners, equall to his expectation, and therfore kendeleth a feruent loue towarde that persone, puttinge all his ioye and delite in the praise and auauncement of him that he loueth, it hapneth that he which is loued, beinge promoted in honour, either of purpose neglecteth his frende, therby suppressynge libertie of speche or familiar resorte; or els esteming his mynde with his fortune onely, and nat with the suertie of frendship, hideth from him the secretes of his harte, and either trusteth no man, or els him whome prosperous fortune hath late brought in acquaintaunce.

d.g: A person's character or inclinations, supposedly determined by their horoscope.
d.x: I knovv thy conſtellation is right apt / For this affayre: […]

constellation.e: PIE word *ḱóm From Middle English constellacioun, constillacioun (“(astrology) position of the moon or a planet in relation to the ascendant sign of the zodiac; horoscope; (astronomy) formation of fixed stars, constellation; (astronomy) elevation or position of the sun”) [and other forms], borrowed from Old French constellation (modern French constellation), or directly from its etymon Late Latin …

d.g: Amazement or horror that confounds the faculties, and incapacitates for reflection; terror, combined with amazement; dismay.
d.x: "Out!" exclaimed her husband, with something like genuine consternation in his voice.

consternation.e: From French consternation, from Latin consternātiō. By surface analysis, consternate + -ion.

d.g: A state of the bowels in which the evacuations are infrequent and difficult, or the intestines become filled with hardened faeces.
d.x: If you also knew how to combine foods—that is, what foods eaten together “set well,” you need never have indigestion, constipation or any of the headachy, stomachachy ills they lead to.

d.g: The act of crowding anything into a lesser space, or the state of being crowded or pressed together; condensation.

constipation.e: First attested in the beginning of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English constipacioun, borrowed from Medieval Latin constīpātiō or its Old French equivalent, from cōnstīpō + -tiō. By surface analysis, constipate + -ion.

d.g: A district represented by one or more elected officials.
d.x: John was elected to parliament from the Bedford constituency.

d.g: The voters within such a district.
The residents of such a district.
The voters of a candidate.

constituency.e: English constituent English -ency English constituency From constituent + -ency.

d.g: The act, or process of setting something up, or establishing something; the composition or structure of such a thing; its makeup.
d.x: the physical constitution of the sun

d.g: The formal or informal system of primary principles and laws that regulates a government or other institutions.
d.x: Our constitution had begun to exist in times when statesmen were not much accustomed to frame exact definitions.

d.g: A legal document describing such a formal system.
A document issued by a religious authority serving to promulgate some particular church laws or doctrines.

constitution.e: PIE word *ḱóm From Middle English constitucioun, constitucion (“edict, law, ordinance, regulation, rule, statute; body of laws or rules, or customs; body of fundamental principles; principle or rule (of science); creation”) from Old French constitucion (modern French constitution), a learned borrowing from Latin cōnstitūtiō, cōnstitūtiōnem (“character, constitution, disposition, nature; definition; point in dispute; order, regulation; arrangement, system”), from cōnstituō (“to establish, set up; to confirm; to decide, resolve”). Equivalent to constitute + -ion.

d.g: A constitutional system of governance.
Adherence to constitutional principles.
Philosophical belief in government under a written constitution.
A person who adheres to the philosophy of constitutionalism.
d.x: It was now getting late, and Mr. Morland summoned them to depart; for he was a constitutionalist in the best sense of the word. It was his own constitution to which he attended.

d.g: A person who is expert in constitutional law.
Of or relating to constitutionalism or its adherents.
Something that constrains; a restriction.
d.x: An engineer must recognize the difference between a constraint (to work within) and a problem (to be eliminated via resolution).

d.g: An irresistible force or compulsion.
d.x: They confessed, but only under severe constraint.

d.g: The repression of one's feelings.
A condition that a solution to an optimization problem must satisfy.

constraint.e: From Middle English constreynt, constreynte, from Old French constreinte, past participle of constreindre (“to constrain”), from Latin cōnstringō (corresponding to the past participle cōnstrictus).

ori.label: Fastening & joining
ori.gloss: binding together; tying, fastening, connecting

origin.label: Fastening & joining
origin.gloss: binding together; tying, fastening, connecting

d.g: The act of constricting, the state of being constricted, or something that constricts.
d.x: The very structural uniqueness of Esperanto makes it hard to translate into ethnic languages – not least because many of those who write in Esperanto do so out of their rejection of the constriction that they experience when writing in their native languages.

d.g: A narrow part of something; a stricture.
d.x: […] greatest breadth at a point about half way between the constriction and the ends […]

d.g: A compression.

constriction.e: Borrowed from Late Latin constrictio, constrictionis, from Latin constringo.

d.g: A muscle whose contraction narrows a vessel or passage or compresses an organ.
Ellipsis of pharyngeal constrictor (“each of the muscles which constrict the pharynx”).
Ellipsis of boa constrictor, either the species Boa constrictor or a similar snake that kills by constriction.

constrictor.e: Borrowed from New Latin cōnstrictor, or from constrict + -or.

d.g: The act of construing: interpreting, portraying, or both.
d.x: Near-synonyms: interpretation, portrayal

d.g: Something constructed from parts.
d.x: The artwork was a construct of wire and tubes.

d.g: A concept or model.
d.x: Bohr's theoretical construct of the atom was soon superseded by quantum mechanics.

d.g: A segment of nucleic acid, created artificially, for transplantation into a target cell or tissue.
To build or form (something) by assembling parts.
d.x: We constructed the radio from spares.

construct.e: Borrowed from Latin cōnstrūctus, from cōnstruō (“to heap together”), from com- (“together”) + struō (“to heap up, pile”). Doublet of construe.

d.g: The process of constructing.
d.x: Construction is underway on the new bridge.

d.g: Anything that has been constructed.
d.x: The engineer marvelled at his construction.

d.g: The trade of building structures.
d.x: He had worked in construction all his life.

d.g: A building, model or some other structure.
d.x: The office was a construction of steel and glass.

construction.e: From Middle English construccioun, construction, from Old French construction, from Latin cōnstructiō, from cōnstruere. Morphologically construct + -ion.

d.g: The characteristic of being constructive.
Creativity, the capacity to invent.

constructiveness.e: English constructive Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English constructiveness From constructive + -nes …

d.g: A Russian movement in modern art characterized by the creation of nonrepresentational geometric objects using industrial materials.
d.x: Constructivism wasn't just Russian state propaganda - its blend of optimism and pragmatism and its emphasis on equality and the collective prefigured key developments in 20th-century art.

d.g: A style of modern architecture that flourished in the Soviet Union in the 1920s and early 1930s.
d.x: Many masterpieces of Soviet constructivism are now crumbling under capitalism, replaced by pastiche architecture or pale replicas of former buildings.

d.g: A philosophy that asserts the need to construct a mathematical object to prove it exists.
d.x: At bottom, constructivism opposes axiomatization as the fundamental idea in mathematics.

d.g: A psychological epistemology which argues that humans generate knowledge and meaning from their experiences.
d.x: According to constructivism, all systems are artificial abstractions. They are not made by nature and presented to use to be discovered, but we construct them by our perceptual and mental capabilities with the domain of our experiences.

d.g: Of or relating to constructivism.
d.x: Social norm scholarship in criminal law, I would suggest, is best understood as a type of constructivist social theory. The emerging literature attempts to explain behavior by focusing on shared interpretations of social practice.

d.g: An advocate of constructivism.
A person who, or thing that, constructs.
d.x: All this time the great work over which South Australia was spending large sums of money, aided by unceasing efforts on the part of her telegraph constructors, was going on.

d.g: A company which, or individual who, builds racing vehicles. In Formula One, constructor status is strictly defined by the rules, but in other motorsports the term is merely a descriptor. Depending on the racing rules, some constructors (e.g. Cosworth) may provide vehicles to racing teams who are not themselves constructors, while others are both teams and constructors (Ducati Corse, Scuderia Ferrari).
A class method that creates and initializes each instance of an object.
A person who creates crossword puzzles.

constructor.e: From Medieval Latin cōnstrūctor, from Latin cōnstruō (“to build”). By surface analysis, construct + -or.

d.g: An identity or union of substance.
The actual, substantial presence of the body of Christ with the bread and wine of the sacrament of the Lord's Supper; impanation, as opposed to transubstantiation.
Custom, familiarity.
d.x: “the stain hath become engrained by time and consuetude; let thy reformation be cautious, as it is just and wise.”

consuetude.e: From Middle English consuetude, from Middle French consuetude, from Old French consuetude, learnedly borrowed from Latin cōnsuētūdō. Doublet of costume, custom, and kastom.

d.g: According to custom; customary; usual.
Synonym of habitual.
d.x: The loss of ye, hath, unto, and a consuetudinal use of be[.]

consuetudinal.e: From Latin cōnsuētūdō (oblique stem cōnsuētūdin-) + -al, from cōnsuēscō + -tūdō, from con- + suēscō. By surface analysis, consuetude + -al.

d.g: A ritual book containing the forms and ceremonies used in the services of a particular monastery, cathedral or religious order.
An unwritten law established by usage, derived by immemorial custom from antiquity.
Customary; considered law by virtue of the fact that it is generally observed.

consuetudinary.e: From Medieval Latin cōnsuetudinārius, from cōnsuētūdō (oblique stem cōnsuētūdin-) + -ārius, from cōnsuēscō + -tūdō, from con- + suēscō. By surface analysis, consuetude + -ary.

d.g: Either of the two heads of government and state of the Roman Republic or the equivalent nominal post under the Roman and Byzantine Empires.
Any of the three heads of government and state of France between 1799 and 1804.
An official residing in major foreign towns to represent and protect the interests of the merchants and citizens of their country.

consul.e: From Middle English consul, from Old English consul, from Latin cōnsul.

d.g: Rule by consuls, as during most periods of the Roman Republic or in France between 1799 and 1804.
The official position and duration held by a consul in diplomatic service.
The business office of a consul; a minor embassy.

consulate.e: From Middle English consulat, consulate, from Latin consulātus, from consul + -ātus. In some senses, via French consulat. By surface analysis, consul + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

d.g: The position and duration held by a consul in their role.

consulship.e: English consul Proto-Germanic *skapjaną Proto-Germanic *-skapiz Proto-West Germanic *-skapi Old English -sċiepe Middle English -schipe English -ship English consulship From consul + -ship.

d.g: A consultant or consulting firm.
d.x: For a PR campaign like never before, one needs a consultancy of unprecedented scope and power.

d.g: The services offered by a consultant.
d.x: I've been doing IT consultancy for three years.

d.g: A person or party that is consulted.

d.g: To injure the brain of, usually temporarily, by violent impact.
d.x: The blow will concuss him.

d.g: To force to do something, or give up something, by intimidation; to coerce.
d.x: The opposite principle , or rather the opposite practice of intrusion , is the reverse of this : it consists in concussing the Presbytery to ordain , and in concussing the people to receive.

concuss.e: From Latin concussus, the perfect passive participle of concutiō (“shake violently”), from con- + quatiō (“shake, hit”).

d.g: To strongly criticise or denounce; to excoriate.
d.x: The president condemned the terrorists.

d.g: To judicially pronounce (someone) guilty.
To judicially announce a verdict upon a finding of guilt; To sentence
d.x: The judge condemned him to death.

d.g: To confer eternal divine punishment upon.

condemn.e: From Middle English condempnen, from Old French condamner, from Latin condemnāre (“to sentence, condemn, blame”), from com- + damnāre (“to harm, condemn, damn”), from damnum (“damage, injury, loss”). Displaced native Middle English fordemen (from Old English fordeman (“condemn, sentence, doom”) > Modern English fordeem.

d.g: To concentrate toward the essence by making more close, compact, or dense, thereby decreasing size or volume.
d.x: An abridged dictionary can be further condensed to pocket size.

d.g: To change from a gas to a liquid state.
d.x: Water condenses on the window on cold days because of the warm air inside.

condense.e: Borrowed from Middle French condenser, from Latin condēnsō.

d.g: To come down from a superior position and do something; to deign; (with a negative connotation) to stoop.
d.x: The boss condescended not to sack him after much persuasion from his coworkers.

d.g: Chiefly followed by on or upon: to go into detail; to particularize, to specify.
To treat (someone) as though inferior; to talk down to (someone); to patronize.
d.x: I didn't mean to condescend you, Mr. Shreck.

condescend.e: From Middle English condescenden, condescendre (“to deign, condescend; to accede graciously; to agree; to agree to, give consent; to make a concession, yield; etc.”), from Old French condescendre (“to descend, go down; to agree or assent to”) (modern French condescendre), from Ecclesiastical Latin condēscendere, the present active infinitive of condēscendō (“to stoop down; to condescend”), from Latin con- (prefix denoting a bringing together of several objects) + dēscendō (“to come or go down, descend; to stoop down”) (from dē- (prefix denoting reversal or undoing) + scandō (“to ascend, mount; to clamber”) (from Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to climb, scale; to dart; to jump; etc.”))).

d.g: Followed by with: to express condolence to, or sympathetic sorrow with, someone; to lament in sympathy with someone.
d.x: […] I doubt Madam, your complaints ought to be turned into acknovvledgments, and your Friends vvould have cauſe to rejoyce rather than condole vvith you; […]

d.g: To express regret or sorrow over (an undesirable event or other misfortune); to bemoan, to grieve, to lament.
d.x: Nay, compaſsion it ſelfe, comes to no great degree, if vvee haue not felt, in ſome proportion, in our ſelues, that vvhich vvee lament and condole in another.

condole.e: PIE word *ḱóm Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin condolēre, the present active infinitive of condoleō (“to feel severe pain, suffer greatly; to suffer with or feel another’s pain, condole”), from Latin con- (prefix denoting a being or bringing together of several things) + doleō (“to suffer physical pain, hurt; to be sorry, grieve for, deplore, lament”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *delh₁- (“to divide, split”)).

d.g: To forgive, excuse or overlook (something that is considered morally wrong, offensive, or generally disliked).
To allow, accept or permit (something that is considered morally wrong, offensive, or generally disliked).
d.x: Rule-utilitarianism is unlikely to condone torturing a child, but it does imply that the torturing of a child is less evil if the torturer shares his pleasure with other sadists-perhaps by inviting an audience, or broadcasting it on the Internet.

d.g: To forgive (marital infidelity or other marital offense).

condone.e: Learned borrowing from Latin condōnāre (“to forgive”).

d.g: To contribute or lead to a specific result.
d.x: The reaſons you alleadge, do more conduce / To the hot paſſion of diſtempred blood, / Then to make vp a free determination / Tvvixt right and vvrong: […]

d.g: be conducive to
To cause (something) to occur; to bring about.
d.x: And vvell aſſured you may be, the King's Highneſs upon Sight of theſe your ſaid Letters, not only much commended your great Diligence and provident Dexterity, in the vviſe conducing of theſe his vveighty Matters, vvhereby ye have deſerved his ſingular Favour and Thanks, but alſo took great Rejoicing, Conſolation and Comfort, in this honourable, princely and loving Demeanour of the ſaid French King: […]

d.g: To contribute (something).
To conduct or lead (someone or something).
d.x: At laſt to conduce things to ſome order out of this Chaos of confuſion, their moſt learned Hiſtorian Elifarni, tooke vpon him to make ſtraight theſe crooked poſtures: […]

d.g: To advantage or benefit (someone or something).
To carry on or continue (an activity).
d.x: VVithin my ſoule there doth conduce a fight / Of this ſtrange nature, that a thing inſeparat, / Diuides more vvider then the skie and earth: […]

d.g: To be advantageous to; to advantage, to benefit.
d.x: So [Julius Caesar] Scaliger of himſelfe ingenuouſly confeſſeth, […] I am mightily detained and allured vvith that grace & comelineſſe of faire vvomen, I am vvell pleaſed to bee idle amongſt them. And vvhat young man is not? As is acceptable and conducing to moſt, ſo eſpecially to a melancholy man.

conduce.e: PIE word *ḱóm From Late Middle English conducen (“to guide, lead; (surgery) to draw together (edges of a wound, or parts of a torn sinew); to set (a broken bone)”), borrowed from Latin condūcere, the present active infinitive of condūcō (“to bring, draw, or lead together, assemble, collect; to contribute to something by being useful, be of use, be conducive to”), from con- (prefix denoting a bringing together of several things) + dūcō (“to conduct, guide, lead, lead away”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to draw, pull; to lead (pull behind oneself)”)). Doublet of conduct and conn.

ori.label: Channels & conduction
ori.gloss: leading fluid, current, heat

origin.label: Channels & conduction
origin.gloss: leading fluid, current, heat

d.g: To speak casually with; to chat.
To confer.
To fabricate memories in order to fill gaps in one's memory.
d.x: "It has been well established that the speech areas in the absence of input often confabulate a response."

confabulate.e: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin cōnfābulātus, perfect active participle of cōnfābulor, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To grant as a possession; to bestow.
d.x: The college has conferred an honorary degree upon the visiting Prime Minister.

d.g: To talk together, to consult, discuss; to collogue.
d.x: They were in a huddle, conferring about something.

d.g: have a conference in order to talk something over

confer.e: From Early Modern English conferre, from Middle French conférer, from Old French conferer, from Latin cōnferō. Compare Dutch confereren, German konferieren, Danish konferere, Swedish konferera. Doublet of collate. See also infer, relate and refer, delate and defer, as well as prelate and prefer among others.

ori.label: Bearing & carrying
ori.gloss: physically bearing or carrying something; movement of bearing

d.g: To admit to the truth, particularly in the context of sins or crimes committed.
d.x: I confess to spray-painting all over that mural!

d.g: To acknowledge faith in; to profess belief in.
d.x: Whosoever, therefore, shall confess me before men, him will I confess, also, before my Father which is in heaven.

d.g: To unburden (oneself) of sins to God or a priest, in order to receive absolution.
d.x: If we confesse our sinnes, hee is faithfull, & iust to forgiue vs our sinnes, and to cleanse vs from all vnrighteousnesse.

d.g: To hear or receive such a confession of sins from.
d.x: A jealous man confesses his wife under a priest's habit, who tells him that she is visited every night by a friar; […]

confess.e: From Middle English confessen, from Anglo-Norman confesser, from Old French confesser, from Latin confessus (Old French confés), past participle of cōnfiteor (“to confess, admit”) from con- + fateor (“to admit”). Displaced Middle English andetten (“to confess, admit”) (from Old English andettan). Doublet of confiteor. Sense 6 is a calque of 告白 (kokuhaku).

d.g: To entrust (something) to the responsibility of someone.
d.x: I confide this mission to you alone.

d.g: To reveal something in private or share secrets with someone.
d.x: I could no longer keep this secret alone; I decided to confide in my brother.

confide.e: From Middle Scots confide, confyde (“to put trust in”), from Latin confīdere (“to put trust in, have confidence in”), from con- (“together”) + fidēre (“to trust”). First attested in English use in the early 17th century. Doublet of faith and fidelity.

d.g: To set up or arrange something in such a way that it is ready for operation for a particular purpose, or to someone's particular liking
d.x: Users may configure the settings to enhance their experience.

configure.e: From Old French configurer, from Latin configurare. See configurate.

d.g: To restrict (someone or something) to a particular scope or area; to keep in or within certain bounds.
d.x: Now let not nature's hand / Keep the wild flood confined! let order die!

d.g: A boundary or limit.
Confinement, imprisonment.
d.x:
She says for you to bring her a slice of cake,
A bottle of the best wine,
And not to forget the fair young lady
That did release you from close confine.

confine.e: From Middle French confiner, from confins, from Medieval Latin confines, from Latin confinium, from confīnis.

d.g: To strengthen; to make firm or resolute.
To administer the sacrament of confirmation on (someone).
d.x: Elizabeth, daughter of Henry VIII, was baptized and confirmed at the age of three days.

d.g: To assure the accuracy of previous statements.
d.x: Despite all the evidence confirming the existence of the Protheans, little is known about their culture and society. From time to time, dig sites will yield new clues, but after 50,000 years of decay, little of value is unearthed.

d.g: To approve a proposal or nomination.
d.x: The Senate must confirm federal court appointments.

confirm.e: From Middle English confirmen, confermen, from Old French confermer, from Latin cōnfirmāre (“to make firm, strengthen, establish”), from con- (“together”) + firmāre (“to make firm”), from firmus (“firm”).

d.g: To catch fire.
To set fire to something.

conflagrate.e: First attested in 1657; borrowed from Latin cōnflāgrātus, perfect passive participial of cōnflāgrō (“to be consumed by fire; (rare) to set aflame”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To combine or mix together.
To fail to properly distinguish or keep separate (things); to mistakenly treat (them) as equivalent.
d.x: “Bacon was Lord Chancellor of England and the first European to experiment with gunpowder.” — “No, you are conflating Francis Bacon and Roger Bacon.”

d.g: To deliberately draw a false equivalence or association, typically in a tacit or implicit manner as propaganda and/or an intentional distortion or misrepresentation of the subject matter.
d.x: But in reality, the order simply furthers the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant policies by continuing to conflate immigration issues with criminal ones.

d.g: Combining elements from multiple versions of the same text.
d.x: Why the redactor created this conflate version, despite its inconsistencies, is a matter of conjecture.

conflate.e: Attested since 1541: from Latin cōnflātus, past passive participle of cōnflō (“fuse, kindle, blow together”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To adapt to something by more closely matching it, especially something normative.
d.x:
There is a worm by Phoebus bred,
By leaves of mulberry is fed,
Which unprovided where to dwell,
Conforms itself to weave a cell.

d.g: To change to more closely match typical characteristics or behavior.
d.x: [H]e had a dispensation for conforming in outward observances to the Protestant faith.

d.g: To be as required or recommended by a specification, regulation, or policy.
d.x: In height and breadth it conformed to the prescribed measurements laid down by the rules of the contest.

conform.e: From Middle English conformen, borrowed from Middle French and Anglo-Norman conformer, from Latin conformāre (“to mould, to shape after”).

d.g: To perplex or puzzle.
d.x: And the brother of Jared being a large and mighty man, and a man highly favored of the Lord, Jared, his brother, said unto him: Cry unto the Lord, that he will not confound us that we may not understand our words.

d.g: To stun or amaze.
To fail to see the difference; to mix up; to confuse right and wrong.
To make something worse.
d.x: Don't confound the situation by yelling.

confound.e: From Middle English confounden (“destroy, ruin, perplex”), from Anglo-Norman cunfundre and Old French confondre, from Latin cōnfundō (“to mingle, mix together”). Related to found (“to melt (metals in a foundry)”) (but not to found (“to start”), nor to find) and to fusion.

d.g: To stand or meet facing, especially in competition, hostility or defiance; to come face to face with.
d.x: It is important that police officers learn to deescalate situations in which someone confronts them aggressively.

d.g: To deal with.
d.x: confront a problem

d.g: To bring someone face to face with something.
d.x: We should confront him about the missing money.

d.g: To come up against; to encounter.
d.x: Inter Milan are to confront Juventus in the final.

confront.e: From Middle French confronter, borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre, from con- + frontem (“front, forehead”).

d.g: to puzzle, perplex, baffle, bewilder (somebody); to afflict by being complicated, contradictory, or otherwise difficult to understand
d.x: It confused me when I went to the office and nobody was there, but then I realised it was Sunday.

d.g: To mix up, muddle up (one thing with another); to mistake (one thing for another).
d.x: People who say "hola" to Italians are confusing Italian with Spanish.

d.g: To mix thoroughly; to confound; to disorder.
d.x: The dense fog utterly confused traffic on the highway.

d.g: To make uneasy and ashamed; to embarrass.

confuse.e: Back-formation from confused, from Middle English confused (“frustrated, ruined”), from Anglo-Norman confus, from Latin cōnfūsus, past participle of cōnfundō.

d.g: prove to be false

confute.e: From Middle French confuter, from Latin confūtō.

d.g: To change from a liquid to solid state, perhaps due to cold; called to freeze in nontechnical usage.
To coagulate, make curdled or semi-solid such as gel or jelly.
To make rigid or immobile.
d.x: We must act before opposition to our plans congeals.

d.g: To become congealed, solidify.

congeal.e: From Middle English congelen, from Middle French congeler, from Latin congelare, cognate with Portuguese and Spanish congelar.

d.g: A farmer whose lands do not support him adequately.
d.x: For quotations using this term, see Citations:congest.

d.g: To hinder or block the passage of something moving, for example a fluid, mixture, traffic, people, etc. (due to an excess of this or due to a partial or complete obstruction), resulting in overfilling or overcrowding.
d.x: congest traffic

d.g: To become blocked or obstructed
d.x: Nasal passages can congest during a cold.

d.g: Shaped like or formed into a ball.
To form into a globe or ball.
d.x: How rich a dower was yours! By how much toil of sinew and of mind Collected, conglobated, were Earth’s stores Treasured in Rome,—the Eternal!—throne assigned By Nature and the Gods for sway of human kind!

conglobate.e: First attested in 1635; borrowed from Latin conglobātus, perfect passive participial of conglobō (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from con- (“together”) + globus (“ball”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix)

d.g: assume a globular shape
To collect (something) into a round mass; to conglobate.
d.x: Not closer, orb in orb, conglob’d are seen / The buzzing Bees about their dusky Queen.

conglobe.e: PIE word *ḱóm From French conglober, from Latin conglobāre, the present active infinitive of conglobō (“to gather into a ball; to accumulate; to crowd together”), from con- (prefix denoting a being or bringing together of several objects) + globus (“round object, globe, sphere; glob; group”) (from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to form into a ball; a ball”)) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs).

d.g: To stick or glue together.
To join together, to unite.
d.x: Bones […] have had their broken parts conglutinated within three or four days.

d.g: Glued together; united, as by some adhesive substance.

conglutinate.e: Inherited from Middle English conglutinaten (“(of a wound, broken bone, etc.) to knit, close up; to fasten; (figurative) to unite”), from conglutinat(e) (used as the past participle of conglutinaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin conglūtinātus, the perfect passive participle of conglūtinō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French conglutiner.

d.g: To express one’s sympathetic pleasure or joy to the person(s) it is felt for
d.x: Remind me to congratulate Dave and Lisa on their wedding.

d.g: To consider oneself fortunate in some matter.
d.x: I congratulated myself on the success of my plan.

congratulate.e: First attested in 1548; borrowed from Latin congrātulātus, the perfect active participle of Latin congrātulor (“to wish joy, rejoice (with); to congratulate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from con- + grātulor, from grātus (“grateful, pleasing, agreeable, beloved”) + -or. By surface analysis, con- + gratulate.

d.g: To collect into an assembly or assemblage; to bring into one place, or into a united body.
d.x: Any multitude of Christian men congregated may be termed by the name of a church.

d.g: To come together; to assemble; to meet.
d.x: Even there where merchants most do congregate.

d.g: Collective; assembled; compact.
d.x: With this reservation, therefore, we proceed to human philosophy or humanity, which hath two parts: the one considereth man segregate or distributively, the other congregate or in society; so as human philosophy is either simple and particular, or conjugate and civil.

congregate.e: The adjective is first attested in 1400–1450, in Middle English, the verb c. 1513; from Middle English congregat(e) (“(of people) banded together; (of liquids) accumulated; (of muscles) contracted; (of wounds) closed up”), borrowed from Latin congregātus, perfect passive participle of congregō (“to congregate”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3), from con- (“with, together”) + gregō (“to collect into a flock”), from grex (“flock, herd”). See gregarious and egregious. Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

d.g: To join together; to unite; to combine.
d.x: They are representatives that will loosely conjoin a nation.

d.g: To marry.
d.x: I will conjoin you in holy matrimony.

d.g: To join as coordinate elements, often with a coordinating conjunction, such as coordinate clauses.
To combine two sets, conditions, or expressions by a logical AND; to intersect.

conjoin.e: From Old French conjoindre, from Latin coniungo, from con- (“together”) + iungo (“join”). Equivalent to con- + join.

d.g: To perform magic tricks.
d.x: He started conjuring at the age of 15, and is now a famous stage magician.

d.g: To summon (a devil, etc.) using supernatural power.
To evoke.
To imagine or picture in the mind.

conjure.e: From Middle English conjuren, from Old French conjurer, from Latin coniūrō (“to swear together; conspire”), from con- (“with, together”) + iūro (“to swear or take an oath”).

d.g: The duty of directing a ship, usually used with the verb to have or to take and accompanied by the article "the."
d.x: The officer of the deck has the conn of the vessel; the captain took the conn when he reached the bridge.

d.g: To direct a ship; to superintend the steering of (a vessel); to watch the course of (a vessel) and direct the helmsman how to steer (especially through a channel, etc, rather than steer a compass direction).
d.x: The pilot conned the ship safely into the harbor.

conn.e: Variant of cond, from Middle English conduen, condien, from Anglo-Norman conduire, from Latin condūcō (“lead, bring or draw together”), from con- (“with, together”) + dūcō (“lead”). Doublet of conduce.

d.g: To join or link two objects together, or one object to another, either directly or through a common intermediary.
d.x: I think this piece connects to that piece over there.

d.g: To arrive at an intended target; to land.
d.x: When that roundhouse kick connected with his temple it sent him flying across the room.

d.g: A drug dealer.
d.x: My connects in Chicago are telling me all kinds of things. Nobody knows anything for sure except that Griffith is missing and money is missing.

d.g: A useful friend or associate.
d.x: Even though I did not have a lot of connects in Silicon Valley, I was not concerned because I knew that Silicon Valley was not going to solve this problem.

connect.e: Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm Proto-Italic *kom Proto-Italic *kom- Latin con- Latin nectō Latin cōnectō Latin connectō English connect From Latin connectere (“fasten together”), from con- (“together”) + nectere (“bind”), which is cognate with English knot and English knit.

d.g: To secretly cooperate with other people in order to commit a crime or other wrongdoing; to collude, to conspire.
d.x: I might say, / That who despairs, acts; that who acts, connives / With God's relations set in time and space; [...]

d.g: Of parts of a plant: to be converging or in close contact; to be connivent.

connive.e: From French conniver (“to ignore and thus become complicit in wrongdoing”), or directly from its etymon Latin con(n)īvēre (“close or screw up the eyes, blink, wink; overlook, turn a blind eye, connive”) (perhaps alluding to two persons involved in a scheme together winking to each other), from con- (prefix indicating a being or bringing together of several objects) + *nīvēre (related to nictō (“to blink, wink”), from Proto-Indo-European *kneygʷʰ- (“to bend, droop”)).

d.g: To signify beyond its literal or principal meaning.
d.x: Racism often connotes an underlying fear or ignorance.

d.g: To possess an inseparable related condition; to imply as a logical consequence.
d.x: Poverty connotes hunger.

d.g: To express without overt reference; to imply.
To require as a logical predicate to consequence.

connote.e: From Medieval Latin connotō (“signify beyond literal meaning”), from com- (“together”), + notō (“mark”).

d.g: To defeat in combat; to subjugate.
d.x: I lay in the desert beyond all cities and sounds, and above me flowed the River of Silence through the sky; and on the desert’s edge night fought against the Sun, and suddenly conquered.

d.g: To acquire by force of arms, win in war; to become ruler of; to subjugate.
d.x: In 1453, the Ottoman Empire conquered Constantinople.

d.g: To overcome an abstract obstacle.
d.x: Today I conquered my fear of flying by finally boarding a plane.

d.g: To gain, win, or obtain by effort.
d.x: to conquer freedom; to conquer a peace

conquer.e: From Middle English conqueren, from Old French conquerre, from Late Latin conquaerere (“to knock, strike; to search for, procure”), from Latin con- + quaerere (“to seek, acquire”). Displaced native Old English oferwinnan.

d.g: To think about seriously.
d.x: Consider that we’ve had three major events and the year has hardly begun.

d.g: To think about something seriously or carefully: to deliberate.
To think about whether one will do (an action); to weigh as a possible course of action.
d.x: I’m considering going to the beach tomorrow.

d.g: To assign some quality to.
d.x: Consider yourself lucky, but consider your opponent skillful.

consider.e: From Middle English consideren, from Middle French considerer, from Latin considerare.

d.g: To transfer to the custody of, usually for sale, transport, or safekeeping.
To entrust to the care of another.
To send to a final destination.
d.x: to consign the body to the grave

d.g: To assign; to devote; to set apart.
d.x: The French commander, charmed with the greatneſs of your ſoul, accordingly conſign’d it [a donation] to the uſe for which it was intended by the donor[…]

consign.e: Borrowed from Middle French consigner or directly from Latin cōnsignō (“furnish with a seal”), from con- + signō (“mark, sign”).

d.g: A lineup or sequence of railroad carriages or cars, with or without a locomotive, that form a unit.
d.x: The train's consist included a baggage car, four passenger cars, and a diner.

consist.e: From Middle French consister, from Latin consistō (“stand together, stop, become hard or solid, agree with, continue, exist”), from com- (“together”) + sistō (“to cause to stand, stand”).

d.g: To unite in an ecclesiastical consociation.

consociate.e: From Latin cōnsociātus, past participle of cōnsociō (“to associate, unite”).

d.g: To combine into a single unit; to group together or join.
d.x: He consolidated his luggage into a single large bag.

d.g: To make stronger or more solid.
d.x: These infamous little green men appeared during the decisive seizures or buildings and facilities, only to disappear when associated militias and local troops arrived to consolidate the gains. In this way they provided a measure of deniability—however superficial or implausible—for Moscow.⁴⁰

d.g: With respect to debt, to pay off several debts with a single loan.

consolidate.e: Borrowed from Latin consolidātus, from the verb consolidō, from solidus (“solid”). By surface analysis, con- + solid + -ate.

d.g: sound in sympathy
To secretly plot or make plans together, often with the intention to bring bad or illegal results; to collude, to connive, to plot.
d.x: They conspired against [Joseph] to slay him.

d.g: To agree, to concur to one end.
d.x: The press, the pulpit, and the stage / Conspire to censure and expose our age.

d.g: To work together to bring about.
d.x: Rain and sweat conspired to smudge her mascara.

conspire.e: From Middle English conspiren, from Old French conspirer, from Latin conspirare, conspīrō, from con- (combining form of cum (“with”)) + spīrō (“breathe”).

d.g: To combine as a cluster.
To fit, adorn (as if) with constellations.
To (form a) cluster.
d.x: It’s no surprise that so much fiction constellates around the subject of Henry and his wives.

d.g: To shine with united radiance, or one general light.

constellate.e: From Latin constēllātus (“starred”), past participle of constēllō. Equivalent to Latin constēllō + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To cause consternation in; to dismay.
To cause constipation in, render costive.
d.x: The medication can constipate you if you’re not drinking enough water.

The idiomatic phrase entered the popular lexicon as part of an advertising slogan in late 1930s or early 1940s, for American Gas Association. The slogan "Now you're cooking with gas!" was coined by Deke Houlgate, an employee of AGA, who worked with Bob Hope to insert the phrase into his comedy routines as subtle product placement. d.x: It remains to explain one final concept, namely what a context free language is. (Don’t get confused: we’ve told you what a context free grammar is, but not what a context free language is.) Quite simply, a context free language is a language that can be generated by a context free grammar. Some languages are context free, and some are not. For example, it seems plausible that English is a context free language. That is, it is probably possible to write a context free grammar that generates all (and only) the sentences that native speakers find acceptable. On the other hand, some dialects of Swiss-German are not context free. It can be proved mathematically that no context free grammar can generate all (and only) the sentences that native speakers of Swiss-German find acceptable.¹ So if you wanted to write a grammar for such dialects, you would have to employ additional grammatical mechanisms, not merely context free rules.

It should also be noted that while the logical form of a property allows for its coinstantiation with a whole host of other properties, it does not allow for coinstantiation with more than one property of a particular type at any one time. Such multiple coinstantiation is excluded as a matter of logic. For instance, and continuing with the preceding example, while the property green may be coinstantiated with the properties soft and hard respectively, it cannot be coinstantiated with each of these at one and the same time because the one logically excludes the other.
